headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risk from shared file/MCP pathways; no direct evidence of a blocked interaction.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A (opik) can call REST APIs and has broad network egress; Agent B (Semantic Kernel) can read/write application-defined files and use MCP servers. That creates a plausible default pathway where B ingests A-produced content or shared workspace artifacts as instructions. No isolation or provenance tracking is documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Agent B reads content produced by Agent A from a shared file or MCP channel without provenance checks, prompt injection is possible.
IF the orchestrator routes A's REST outputs into B's tool prompts, B may follow attacker-controlled instructions.
mitigations: Disable shared file handoff between the agents.
Add provenance tags and reject untrusted instruction-like text.
Route A outputs through a sanitizer before B consumes them.
Require explicit allowlists for MCP resources.
requires-engineering: add content-type separation between data and instructions.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B explicitly reads and writes files and handles plugin credentials; Agent A has broad network egress and calls REST APIs. If they share a workspace, A can place sensitive context into files that B reads and then transmits onward. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, but B's file access makes leakage plausible enough to rate medium.
conditions: IF both agents share any filesystem or application-defined workspace, B can read artifacts created by A.
IF B forwards file contents to Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Hugging Face, or MCP servers, those contents may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Store secrets outside any shared directory.
Block file ingestion for sensitive folders.
Review outbound destinations for B's plugins.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls on shared storage.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has broad network egress and REST API access, while B has broad network egress plus filesystem read/write and MCP use. There is overlap on networked actions, but B cannot modify git state or execute shell, and no shared mutable resource is documented. The main conflict is limited to concurrent writes to application files if they are co-located.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same application-defined files, write collisions can occur.
IF an orchestrator maps both agents to the same mutable API quota or plugin state, contention may occur.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Serialize writes to shared artifacts.
Use per-agent API keys.
Avoid shared git worktrees.
requires-engineering: add locking around mutable shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B's plugin-and-agent pattern can treat upstream outputs as inputs, and A can emit REST-backed content without any documented verification step between them. If A's output is consumed as authoritative by B, errors can cascade into downstream actions or generated responses. The profiles do not show direct action authority, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF B uses A's output as a prompt or tool argument without validation, errors can propagate.
IF B's plugins act on A-generated facts, downstream actions may be wrong.
mitigations: Insert a verification step before B consumes A output.
Require citations or structured schemas from A.
Flag low-confidence A outputs for human review.
Limit B to read-only actions until validation passes.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: B handles model provider API keys and plugin credentials and can send data to Azure OpenAI/OpenAI/Hugging Face/MCP servers, while A has broad network egress and REST API access. If regulated or sensitive data enters B, it may flow to third-party services without a documented residency or retention boundary. A is open-source and not itself a compliance blocker, so the risk is driven mainly by B.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into B's application context, it may be sent to external model providers or MCP servers.
IF the deployment lacks a DPA or residency controls for those providers, compliance exposure increases.
mitigations: Restrict regulated data from B's context.
Use region-locked providers only.
Review retention settings for each provider.
Document a DPA before processing sensitive data.
requires-engineering: implement data-class routing and residency enforcement.
